canberra.title: Infrastructure Canberra head will leave the public service before Christmas
canberra.snippet: A second ACT Government directorate will have to find a new leader, with Infrastructure Canberra director-general Gillian Geraghty announ...
canberra.content:
2 October 2026

Start the conversation

Infrastructure Canberra Director-General Gillian Geraghty is leaving the ACT public service. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

A second ACT Government directorate will have to find a new leader, with Infrastructure Canberra director-general Gillian Geraghty announcing her resignation on Friday (2 October).

She informed employees that she’ll leave the ACT Public Service and the directorate in early December.

“In a message to employees, Ms Geraghty reflected on her time with the organisation, expressed her gratitude for the commitment and contribution of staff, and said she looked forward to thanking colleagues personally over the coming weeks before her departure,” an ACT Government statement read.

Ms Geraghty was appointed Director-General of Major Projects Canberra in September 2023. The organisation was later expanded and was renamed to Infrastructure Canberra in November 2024.

In February 2024, Ms Geraghty was also appointed ACT Chief Engineer by Engineers Australia in addition to her role as Director-General.

During her tenure, Ms Geraghty oversaw delivery of major ACT Government infrastructure projects including the CIT Woden Campus, Yurauna Centre, Woden Youth Foyer, Woden Interchange and the Canberra Hospital Expansion.

Acting Head of Service Russ Campbell paid tribute to Ms Geraghty’s contribution to the ACT Public Service, acknowledging her leadership of Infrastructure Canberra and her role as ACT Chief Engineer.

“[She has] overseen the delivery of major infrastructure projects across education, housing, transport and health, and had helped strengthen the Territory’s approach to infrastructure planning and delivery, engineering assurance, procurement, workforce capability and stewardship of the government estate,” the ACT Government statement read.

Opposition Leader Mark Parton questioned the timing of the announcement, hot off the heels of Head of Service Kathy Leigh’s announcement she’ll also retire earlier this week and the Health and Community Services Directorate opening a voluntary redundancy program.

“This has been another week of chaos, dysfunction and crisis for the ACT Labor Government,” he said.

“This is what happens when a government has been in power for almost 25 years and loses its focus on basic accountability, financial discipline and good administration. The senior leadership are walking out, public servants are being asked to accept redundancies, and taxpayers are being asked to foot the bill for years of poor decision-making.

“Canberrans deserve a government that is in control and puts them first, not one constantly managing the consequences of its own dysfunction.”

Ms Geraghty’s final day will be 4 December.

canberra.title: Severe storms strike NSW, authorities warn of flash flooding, damaging winds and hail
canberra.snippet: Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain is expected to hit much of the state over the long weekend, with the SES warning communities across G...
canberra.content:
2 October 2026

Start the conversation

The SES is warning communities to be on high alert, with severe weather expected in coming days. Photo: NSW SES.

Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain is expected to hit much of the state over the long weekend, with the SES warning communities across Greater Sydney, Illawarra, Riverina, North Coast and southern NSW to be on high alert.

Emergency services are preparing for extreme weather in the coming days with forecast storms at risk of bringing flash flooding, damaging winds, large hail and heavy rainfall of up to 100 mm in some parts of NSW.

“We are closely monitoring the forecast alongside our partner agencies and will continue to adjust our operations as conditions develop,” NSW SES Acting Assistant Commissioner Brigid Rice said.

“Flash flooding remains our biggest concern during this forecast weather.

“Conditions can change very quickly, and roads that appear safe can become dangerous within minutes.”

A cold front is predicted to bring widespread thunderstorms to the Central West, South Coast, Illawarra and Sydney until Sunday (4 October), before moving north-east early next week.

NSW SES is calling on residents in these areas to monitor the forecast and warnings and take preventative actions such as securing loose outdoor items that could become airborne in strong winds, parking vehicles undercover or away from trees where possible and cleaning gutters and drains to improve water flow around homes.

“By taking a few simple steps today and staying informed throughout the weekend, people can reduce their risk and be ready to act if conditions worsen,” Acting Assistant Commissioner Rice said.

“I encourage people to download the Hazards Near Me app to stay across the latest warnings and information, monitor forecasts on the Bureau of Meteorology and follow the advice of emergency services.”

While authorities are on standby to respond to calls for assistance, the community is being urged to act safely and responsibly to minimise the risk.

“Never drive, ride or walk through floodwater,” Acting Assistant Commissioner Rice said.

“Floodwater often hides damage, debris and other hazards beneath the surface.”

For assistance during floods and storms call the NSW SES on 132 500, or in a life-threatening emergency call triple zero.

Original Article published by Keeli Dyson on Region Illawarra.

canberra.title: Woman killed on Monaro Highway remembered as ‘a real joy’
canberra.snippet: Tributes have poured in for a woman described as “everyone’s champion”, following her death on the Monaro Highway. Jane...
canberra.content:
Jane Faulder, 60, died after being struck by a vehicle. Photo: Queanbeyan Players Inc. Facebook.

Tributes have poured in for a woman described as “everyone’s champion”, following her death on the Monaro Highway.

Jane Faulder, 60, died after being struck by a vehicle on Friday (25 September).

A NSW Police spokesperson said that at about 6:30 pm, emergency services were called to the Monaro Highway after reports a woman had been hit by a vehicle about one kilometre south of Bredbo.

Paramedics treated Ms Faulder, but she died at the scene.

Friend Jen Hinton wasn’t surprised by the outpouring of tributes following her death.

“She was known across the community,” she told Region.

“I think it just goes back to her personality. She was such a really fun person to be around – hardworking, just a real joy to have in the room.”

The two women met through the theatre group Queanbeyan Players.

Ms Hinton was a musical director for three shows – productions of Guys and Dolls, South Pacific and The Sound of Music – where she worked alongside Ms Faulder.

“She’s been a well-loved member of the theatre community in Canberra and the surrounds.

“She was just such a vibrant person … She was just such an awesome person.”

When Ms Hinton thinks of Ms Faulder, she remembers her kindness, including for animals and her fellow humans.

“She was the sort of person that would take people under her wing in productions as well, [especially] younger people.

“She was a friend to everyone. I can’t think of anyone who disliked Jane. In the theatre community, that’s sometimes a bit of a novel [thing].

“Everyone loved Jane. That’s one of the things that I would say. No one ever had a bad word to say about her.”

Ms Hinton remembers Ms Faulder as one of the “hardest working” cast members, who was always able to diffuse negative energy in a room.

“She was such a vibrant person – and she was funny, too.”

The Deanne Calisthenics Club paid tribute to Ms Faulder, who was a member of their Masters team.

“Her warmth, friendship and contribution to our club and the wider calisthenics community will be remembered fondly by so many,” they said.

“We extend our deepest sympathies to Jane’s family and friends, and to her many fellow calisthenics team members and all those who had the privilege of knowing her.

Ms Faulder is being remembered for her involvement in several causes. Image: Calisthenics ACT Facebook.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Calisthenics ACT (CaliACT) said Ms Faulder would be “missed deeply” and “remembered with gratitude”.

“Jane was a cherished part of our community for over 50 years, known for her dedication to our sport, her warm spirit, and the way she gave of herself so generously.

“Across her many roles: performer, volunteer and steadfast supporter, Jane shaped our community with kindness, commitment, and a genuine love for calisthenics. She lifted others up, celebrated their achievements, and brought joy and encouragement wherever she went.”

Ms Faulder was a life member of CaliACT, served on Club and CaliACT committees, and worked to establish the ACT Solo Grading Committee.

The Australian Calisthenic Federation described her as “everyone’s champion”.

“She was the first to lift others up, cheering on competitors from every club and celebrating their successes,” they said.

A NSW Police spokesperson said the driver of the vehicle, a 54-year-old man, was uninjured and was taken to hospital for mandatory testing.

Investigations are ongoing.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Bikie-busting police squad allegedly uncovers weapons, drugs and Comanchero clothes
canberra.snippet: Comanchero outlaw motorcycle gang-branded clothes were seized when police investigated an alleged drug dealer this week. As part of the b...
canberra.content:
2 October 2026

Police seized this Comanchero OMCG-labelled vest during a raid this week. Photo: ACT Policing.

Comanchero outlaw motorcycle gang-branded clothes were seized when police investigated an alleged drug dealer this week.

As part of the bikie-busting Taskforce Invidia’s ongoing investigation into drug trafficking in the ACT, its officers were joined by tactical police when raiding a home in Kambah on Thursday (1 October).

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the raid allegedly uncovered numerous weapons including two machetes, a tomahawk axe, three tasers, two batons, a set of knuckledusters and various bladed weapons.

Also, police allegedly found 35 grams of a crystalline substance believed to be methamphetamine, two vials of clear liquid suspected to be steroids, as well as clothing and paraphernalia related to the Comancheros.

Matti Kemppainen, a 36-year-old of Kambah, was arrested and charged with six counts of possessing a prohibited weapon without authorisation and one count of drug trafficking.

He briefly appeared in the ACT Magistrates Court on Friday (2 October), but did not apply for bail, and it was formally refused before he was remanded into custody.

The matter was adjourned to 9 October. No pleas were entered.

“Further investigations are ongoing,” the police spokesperson said.

canberra.title: Drunk driver’s night on booze ends with him crashing car into house
canberra.snippet: A drunk driver was so intoxicated that it was surprising he was even able to stand when he got behind the wheel of a car and crashed into...
canberra.content:
2 October 2026

John Biar Abit Biar, 27, received a suspended sentence and was released from custody before police apprehended him again. Photo: Albert McKnight.

A drunk driver was so intoxicated that it was surprising he was even able to stand when he got behind the wheel of a car and crashed into a house.

But John Biar Abit Biar did not stop and apologise after narrowly avoiding injuring or killing the residents of the home. Instead, he drove off, perhaps hoping no one would notice the severe damage to his car.

The 27-year-old was convicted and sentenced to one year and three months’ jail by the ACT Magistrates Court on Thursday (1 October), with the sentence suspended after he spent five months behind bars.

The court heard he was driving a friend’s car on 23 April 2026 when he lost control in Holt, drove through a property’s Colorbond fence and crashed into the house, causing extensive damage to the building.

“He knew he was intoxicated and he still chose to drive a car, and this is the result,” prosecutor Chamil Wanigaratne said.

“It is only by good fortune that no one was significantly injured or killed as a result of his driving.”

Biar then drove back to the home of a friend, where he was staying. Police arrived to find the badly damaged car parked in the driveway.

He was arrested at the property and returned a blood alcohol concentration sample of 0.284 – more than five times the legal driving limit.

“I’m surprised he could actually stand, let alone drive a car,” Mr Wanigaratne said.

But he accepted there was no evidence Biar had intentionally driven towards the house before the crash.

John Biar Abit Biar is met by police officers waiting outside the ACT Courts on Thursday. Photo: Albert McKnight.

Biar’s lawyer, Donovan Kelso of Legal Aid, said it was the first time his client had committed offences and that he had caused the serious accident after becoming uncharacteristically drunk, then making a foolish decision to drive.

He also said his client had been unable to contact his wife and two children during the five months he had spent behind bars.

The court heard that Biar was born in South Sudan, moved to Australia in 2002, worked in construction in Adelaide and Melbourne, and planned to live in Adelaide with his aunt after his release.

Magistrate Ian Temby noted he hadn’t appeared to have verbalised any empathy for the victims. But he also said there didn’t appear to be any need for his rehabilitation.

Biar pleaded guilty to two counts of damaging property and one count of dangerous driving.

He had remained in custody since he was arrested after the crash.

Because he had already spent five months in jail, he was released after sentencing on Thursday to complete a two-year good behaviour order.

However, he was arrested again by police officers waiting outside the ACT Courts as he was leaving, as they were planning to apply to extradite him to South Australia to face unrelated charges.

australia.title: Bruce Baird, former federal Liberal MP and NSW minister, dies aged 84
australia.snippet: Baird, father of former NSW premier Mike Baird and journalist Julia Baird, helped win the Olympics for Sydney Get our breaking news email...
australia.content:
Bruce Baird, a former federal Liberal MP and deputy leader of the party’s New South Wales branch, has died aged 84.

Baird, who also served as the NSW transport minister from 1988 to 1995, is the father of former state premier Mike Baird, the ABC journalist Julia Baird, and the marketing executive Steve Baird.

As a NSW minister, Baird was instrumental in lobbying for the 2000 Olympic Games to be based in Sydney. He then entered federal parliament as the member for Cook.

Baird retired before the 2007 election, when Scott Morrison won the seat and went on to become prime minister.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Morrison said Baird was “a giant, a mentor and a friend who celebrated and lived out his strong Christian faith, loved his family and served his country, his state and our community in the shire”.

“His achievements are significant, most notably the transforming effect he had on our home city of Sydney as the minister for Sydney’s successful Olympic bid. But there are many more.”

NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, said Baird was “driven by a strong sense of service, conviction, and compassion, earning the trust and respect of people regardless of their political affiliation”.

“Above all, Bruce was a devoted husband to his late wife Judy, and a proud father and grandfather.”

In a statement, a NSW Liberal spokesperson offered its “deepest condolences on behalf of all members to his family at this difficult time”.

Baird was a passionate supporter of refugees and advocated on their behalf throughout his career.

While a Liberal MP, he opposed the Howard government’s mandatory detention of asylum seekers. After leaving office, he became a member of Kevin Rudd’s refugee resettlement advisory council.

In 2010, Baird criticised the reopening of Curtin detention centre in Western Australia to house asylum seekers.

“Don’t confuse treating people badly when they arrive with effective border control mechanisms, they are two different things,” he told the ABC.

“If we rely on treating asylum seekers badly in this country then there is something about us that we need to have a hard look at. I don’t believe that is the Australian way.”

Baird was also a regular feature of Manly’s Bold and Beautiful ocean swimming club. A member of the squad also confirmed his death on Friday.

On Thursday, the club’s organiser, Peter Anthony, wrote to members describing Baird as a “wonderful friend to so many of us”.

australia.title: OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia
australia.snippet: Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday Get our breaking news...
australia.content:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia.

In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into a New South Wales state government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.

The breach, which comes weeks after news of a similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data, was not reported by the US based company until Thursday.

The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach.

The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service.

OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available.

The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office.

“The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences.

“We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said.

Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week.

“We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said.

On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date.

The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June.

The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent.

An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools.

australia.title: Activists plan legal action against police ban on entering security zone near Perth weapons expo
australia.snippet: Under new WA laws anyone who defies an exclusion order could face a maximum $36,000 fine and three years in prison Get our breaking news ...
australia.content:
Activists and a Greens MP have threatened legal action after the Western Australia police banned at least 12 people entering a designated security area where the Land Forces weapons expo will be held in Perth from 6 October.

The police used special powers given to them by the WA government last month to ban the activists from entering the area surrounding the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre.

Two of the activists, 18-year-old Will Shanahan and 22-year-old Matilda Lane-Rose, said in a media conference held with the Greens MP Sophie McNeill on Friday they would take legal action if police and the police minister, Reece Whitby, did not revise the ban.

“We’ve sought legal advice, and we think that we have standing to pursue a judicial review into this decision,” said Lane-Rose, who works as a staffer for McNeill.

Lane-Rose told reporters the police called her on Thursday saying she had been placed on the exclusion list, despite having no plans to attend the protest against the expo, which is being organised by the WA Anti-War Collective.

The legislation used to ban her and 11 others, called the Land Forces (Special Powers) Bill 2026 was passed last month. It gives police expanded stop-and-search powers and the ability to ban people from entering a security zone that extends from the Elizabeth Quay bus port to the convention centre for 10 days.

Anyone who defies an exclusion order could face a maximum $36,000 fine and three years in prison.

The Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition event is held every two years and is Australia’s biggest weapons expo. The last event was held in 2024 in Melbourne, and attracted a large protest where police were accused of using excessive force.

Melbourne activists Violet Coco and Brad Homewood are among the 12 people issued an exclusion order by WA police.

The companies expected to exhibit at the expo are not listed on the Landforces website. Last month McNeill made public the list, which included an Australian subsidiary of Israel’s largest weapons company, Elbit Systems, and the state-owned company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.

The two companies have been criticised by a former member of the UN commission of inquiry, Chris Sidoti, for being “key enablers of the Israel Defense Forces in its commission of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza over the last two years”.

Whitby said in response to the protesters comments: “We want Land Forces to be a safe and secure environment for attendees, workers, exhibitors, protestors and the wider community.

“These powers are preventative in nature and are intended to deter dangerous or disruptive behaviour before it occurs.

“Each excluded person has a demonstrated history of posing a serious threat to people and/or property.”

McNeill accused the government of using the legislation to target peaceful climate activists.

“They said that these powers were for people who had the propensity to commit violence, people who are a threat to the community,” she said.

“Instead, what we’ve seen is peaceful activists targeted … who didn’t even have any plans to be here in Perth next week. It’s outrageous.”

Shanahan, who recently moved to Newcastle from Perth, said they had not intended to attend the protest given they no longer lived in Western Australia, but now planned to do so, to defy the ban.

“I cannot sit and watch my home state be captured by global militarisation and be turned into an all-out police state,” Shanahan said.

Lane-Rose was fined $2,000 last year after pleading guilty with other Disrupt Burrup Hub activists to attempted trespass and criminal damage at the home of the then Woodside boss, Meg O’Neill, in 2023.

The WA police were approached for comment.

australia.title: Shoebridge pledges Greens members will ‘have a say’ in next leader – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A Sydney man has been charged after allegedly restra...
australia.content:
‘PM deserves pay justice too’: union leader

Henry Belot

A union leader campaigning for public servants to be paid more by the federal government says the prime minister is vastly underpaid.

Earlier today, Guardian Australia reported on 11 public servants being paid more than $1m, which is significantly more than the prime minister’s base wage of $622,000. One public servant was paid more than $1.5m.

Jeff Lapidos, who leads a branch of the Australian Services Union that represents Tax Office staff, has spent more than a decade fighting for better pay and conditions. He has also seen significant job cuts.

When asked about the Future Fund salaries, Lapidos said he did not believe in common salary levels across the public service. He said officials should instead be paid for the value of their work.

After inflation, the value of ATO employees’ salaries has fallen by 9.55% over the last 13 years. This is disgraceful exploitation by successive Coalition and Labor governments.

The ASU is campaigning for pay justice for all ATO staff. The prime minister deserves pay justice too. His office is vastly underpaid.

The prime minister’s salary is set by an independent remuneration tribunal.

Key events

  • 6h ago

    What we learned, Friday 2 October

  • 8h ago

    ‘PM deserves pay justice too’: union leader

  • 9h ago

    Shoebridge says party members will get input into leadership changes

  • 10h ago

    Coalition rails against ATO's decision to stop taking credit card payments

  • 10h ago

    Israeli embassy condemns ‘flydubai false flag’ conspiracies

  • 11h ago

    NSW police allege two women targeted in ‘excessively violent’ home invasions

  • 12h ago

    Victoria set for ‘much more’ rainfall after period of wild weather

  • 13h ago

    Labor to make it harder for international students to 'course hop'

  • 14h ago

    Man charged with sexually assaulting woman in Sydney park

  • 15h ago

    eSafety commissioner says ‘time for new leadership’ after 10 years in role

  • 16h ago

    Online gaming 'shortcomings' put children at risk, eSafety report finds

What we learned, Friday 2 October

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the week.

Before we go, let’s recap today’s top headlines:

  • “Visa hopping” international students, migration agents and lawyers trying to “game” the migration system will be targeted by the federal government, as Labor unveils a further crackdown.

  • NSW police believe two women who were allegedly assaulted and robbed during separate home invasions were targeted in premeditated attacks.

  • Israeli embassy condemned “flydubai false flag” conspiracies theories circulating online about the alleged flydubai attack.

  • New Greens leader, David Shoebridge, says ordinary party members will have input into the next leadership decision, pledging a “conversation” to occur across branches and membership.

  • Online gaming services are failing to take enough action to prevent children being exposed to harmful content, a new report from the eSafety Commissioner has found. More on eSafety Commissioner, Julie Inman-Grant, who confirmed this morning “it’s probably time for new leadership” at the body after serving 10 years in the role.

  • A union leader campaigning for public servants to be paid more by the federal government says the prime minister is vastly underpaid. Earlier today, Guardian Australia reported on 11 public servants being paid more than $1m, which is significantly more than the prime minister’s base wage of $622,000.

  • The Coalition is railing against news the Australian Tax Office will no longer accept credit card payments from 20 November 2026.

  • Significant rainfall is expected to continue across much of Victoria, which has already been battered by storms and flash flooding.

Thanks for sticking around, have a lovely weekend!

Julian Hill backs Chris Minns’ comments on pace of migration

Assistant citizenship minister Julian Hill has backed comments made by the NSW premier, Chris Minns, about the pace of migration into Australia post-Covid.

During an appearance on Kylie Sandilands’ show, Minns said he believed “too many people came into the country in too short a space of time” in the years after Covid.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hill said he had not seen the specific comments but “broadly” agreed with them, while adding there were “a couple of nuanced points”.

Post-Covid – remember when the government was elected in 2022 coming out of Covid – we have the lowest unemployment in our country for over 50 years and employers right across the country, whether cafes, farmers, businesses were screaming out for warm human bodies who could be workers.

That was the big reason why net overseas migration peaked a bit too high post-Covid is the border reopened and fell a bit too slowly because fewer people were leaving.

A series of changes since coming to office to get net overseas migration down from a peak, it has fallen by about 50% and it needs to fall a bit further to get back to a sensible balance and give housing a chance to catch up.

Ima Caldwell

Daylight saving starts this weekend. Here’s what you need to know.

It’s that time of year again: clocks will move forward one hour on Sunday in many parts of Australia as daylight saving time comes into effect.

Here’s all you need to know – and how it will affect you:

Medibank facing dual court actions over data hack

Federal court justice Jonathan Beach heard evidence on Friday to help decide whether two separate cases against Medibank will be held jointly or as separate trials, AAP reports.

The health insurer is facing both a class action by affected customers and civil penalties brought by the privacy watchdog over the 2022 hack.

After Medibank declined to pay a ransom, personal data was leaked on the dark web under malicious file names, including boozy, STD and psycho.

A lawyer for the class action argued it was in the interests of justice to hear the cases together. Wendy Harris KC said.

The technical issues here overlap and intersect at multiple stages … in terms of the architecture of Medibank’s cybersecurity systems [and] the control deficiencies in them.

Neil Young KC, who is representing Medibank in both matters, called the class action a “total mess”, saying it went well beyond the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner’s case in its allegations of cybersecurity failures.

There are many new allegations of breach.

In order for us to address those new allegations, that’s going to require time.

Beach adjourned the matter until 16 October, in part to allow the class action party to consolidate its statement of claim.

Achol Arok

Good afternoon! l’ll be here to take the reins.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Achol Arok will take things from here and guide you into the weekend.

ANZ ends relationship with KPMG

A big four bank is ending its relationship with its auditor of nearly six decades in the latest fallout from a whistleblower scandal, AAP reports.

KPMG has been ANZ’s auditor since 1969 and while the partners who worked on the audit have regularly rotated, the bank is looking for a new firm.

“A tenure of this length is no longer considered appropriate and has been under consideration by the board for some time,” ANZ said in a statement on Friday.

ANZ will begin a competitive tender process to select a new auditor beginning with the 2028-29 financial year.

The tender process will wind up in April and KPMG won’t be eligible to participate, the bank said. KPMG earned $21.4m for auditing and reviewing ANZ’s accounts in 2024-25, with its total fees, including non-audit services, coming to $29.6m for that financial year.

Shoebridge says party members will get input into leadership changes

Josh Butler

New Greens leader David Shoebridge says ordinary party members will have input into the next leadership decision, pledging a “conversation” to occur across branches and membership.

The Greens’ party room chooses its federal leader, which is the same as the Liberal and Nationals, but unlike Labor, which has a party room and membership vote. Shoebridge said this week, in announcing his leadership tilt, that he supported membership having a say; Mehreen Faruqi, who was unsuccessful in her leadership candidacy, said after the party room vote that she wanted members to have input.

In a social media video this afternoon, with the caption “your say on Greens leadership”, Shoebridge said: “You absolutely should have a say in the leadership for the Greens”.

“The good news is Steph [Hodgins-May] and I are gonna make this happen,” he said.

Shoebridge didn’t commit to any specific type of model, but said it would be “a conversation we’re going to have right across the Greens. Every state and territory, hundreds and hundreds of branches, thousands and thousands of members, because members want to be engaged in this.”

Shoebridge committed that the change would happen “before we make the next decision on the federal leadership”, which under Greens rules, happens after every federal election – so, in other words, in this term of parliament.

City of Yarra mayor cleared of assault allegation at election party

A prominent mayor has been cleared of punching a community activist who had gatecrashed his election after-party, Australian Associated Press reports.

The City of Yarra mayor Stephen Jolly, 64, said he was relieved to be acquitted of unlawful assault after Melbourne magistrate Jill Prior handed down her decision on Friday.

Jolly, whose council includes Carlton North, Collingwood and Richmond, fought the charge at a contested hearing, denying he intentionally struck activist Estella Burrows in the face on 1 November 2024.

Burrows and two other masked protesters had gatecrashed Jolly’s election after-party at a Collingwood venue, holding a banner and using a megaphone to accuse Jolly of abuse.

It was alleged Jolly punched Burrows to the face as he and other attendees forced the group to leave. The mayor denied intentionally hitting Burrows and separately argued he was acting in self-defence.

The magistrate on Friday determined Jolly did strike the left side of Burrows but she could not be satisfied he did so intentionally.

It was possible Jolly had been trying to disarm the group of their megaphone or he was reaching forward to move them away, the magistrate determined.

As a result, she found Jolly not guilty of the unlawful assault charge.

Outside court, Burrows told reporters she was disappointed but not surprised at the decision, claiming the justice system only worked in the favour of powerful white men.

This crocodile just predicted the winner of the NRL grand final

Elvis the saltwater crocodile has his prediction for the winner of the NRL grand final: the Newcastle Knights.

The Australian Reptile Park gave Elvis the choice between the Knights and the Sydney Roosters (in the form of two pieces of meat dangled from sticks).

We’ll see if his prophecy comes true.

Death row inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections in Tennessee – The Latest

The convicted murderer Christa Pike, sentenced to death, has survived two lethal injections and was taken to hospital.

Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in 200 years.

A last-minute appeal to stop the lethal injection was overturned by the supreme court, but the state governor, Bill Lee, has suspended executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year.

Lucy Hough speaks to the attorney and anti-capital punishment campaigner Clive Stafford Smith about the case in The Latest.

australia.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial: victim’s family cries as double murder trial hears triple-zero call
australia.snippet: Court hears audio of call made on morning Luke Davies and Jesse Baird were allegedly murdered by NSW police officer Warning: graphic imag...
australia.content:
A triple-zero call made the morning Luke Davies and his partner Jesse Baird were allegedly murdered has been played to the court as photos of surfboard bags containing their bodies were released.

The recording was aired in the New South Wales supreme court on Friday during the double murder trial of former Sydney police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Davies and Baird with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC told the court a call had been made to the emergency line from Davies’ phone at 9.50am on Friday 19 February 2024.

In the recording, movement can be heard before a muffled voice says “fuck off”. The call then drops out.

An attempt to call back goes straight to voicemail where Davies says: “Hi, you’ve reached Luke, please leave a message and I’ll get back to you.”

The Davies family cried in court as the audio played.

Police were sent to patrol the vicinity but were unable to pinpoint the exact address where the call originated.

Earlier on Friday, Ben Higginson, who served with the NSW police force criminal investigation team in Sydney, told the court about working with Lamarre-Condon the day before Davies and Baird were killed.

The two police officers had been working at a pro-Palestine protest on 18 February 2024 when Lamarre-Condon asked Higginson about work.

Higginson replied that it had been a “bit of a rough time” as he had been investigating the murder of Lilie James.

James, 21, was a water polo coach at St Andrews Cathedral school who was killed by Paul Thijssen in October 2023 days after the pair broke up.

CCTV captured Thijssen following James into the school’s gymnasium with a hammer before her body was found. He later killed himself at the Vaucluse cliffs.

Higginson became emotional when discussing the case with Lamarre-Condon, noting the crime had occurred at his old school, so it “hit home a bit more”, the court was told on Friday.

But when Lamarre-Condon asked about James’s murder he seemed “blase”, Higginson told the court.

“He thought Paul was stupid for doing it on CCTV,” the police investigator said.

Higginson told the court that Lamarre-Condon then asked if Thijssen hadn’t committed suicide “would he have gotten away with it?”

The investigator said police didn’t only rely on CCTV when examining a crime.

Higginson brought up the 2007 death of Matthew Leveson and told Lamarre-Condon he “could remember the CCTV of [Leveson’s] partner at Bunnings buying tarp, and he ended up burying him in the national park”.

Both police officers then spoke about how cash was more difficult to trace than bank cards and “what avenues detectives look at for suspicious deaths”, the court heard.

When Lamarre-Condon asked about phones, Higginson said he responded: “If you were to leave your phone at home and commit a murder, the phone would be showing up in the vicinity of your residence.”

The defence lawyer John Stratton SC said during his opening statement that Baird and Davies were fatally shot in “self-defence” after struggles with the policeman.

Lamarre-Condon immediately began cleaning up the scene because he “panicked”, the jury was told.

CCTV played to the on Thursday court showed Lamarre-Condon buying a second surfboard bag.

In the footage, the officer walks straight to the surfboard section of the Decathlon in Miranda Westfield, picks up a cover and pays in cash.

Baird’s housemate, known to the court under the pseudonym Sarah King, told the jury on Friday about returning home from work on the night of the alleged murders.

Their other housemate had sent a photo of red liquid, that she believed to be rusted water, underneath surfboard bags and tarp in their back courtyard and sent a photo to King.

King later looked at them, took a photo, and poked one of the bags.

Asked by the prosecution what it felt like, she said: “it just sounded like a tarp”.

Davies and Bairds’ bodies would be found days later in two surfboard covers near the fence line of a monastery in Bungonia.

The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

world.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
world.snippet: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric cla...
world.content:
On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.

Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.

But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.

Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.

The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.

Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.

“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.

“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”

Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.

One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.

“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.

“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.

This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.

“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”

Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.

They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.

“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.

Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.

“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.

  • This article is published in collaboration with Egab

world.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
world.snippet: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left befor...
world.content:
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.

On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing on Brazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds.

The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse.

The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.

The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.

world.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
world.snippet: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women South Africa’s president has called on men to take mo...
world.content:
South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.

Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.

In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.

“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”

South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.

Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.

He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.

“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.

“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”

Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.

Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.

“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”

Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”

They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

world.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
world.snippet: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy Burundi has agreed to join a clutc...
world.content:
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.

“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.

Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.

The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

world.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
world.snippet: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says A senior member of t...
world.content:
A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.

The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.

Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.

The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.

First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.

Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.

Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.

Reuters contributed to this report
